coverage.heading: What this is about
coverage.answer: Pueblo's next Essential Air Service (EAS) provider selection, a public engagement event and the future of scheduled air service; not a closure notice. [S1,S2]

coverage.heading: The main finding
coverage.answer: Denver Air Connection's existing order runs to March 31, 2027. The public can give input at an announced December 15 open house. Neither a new winner nor the 2027 subsidy is known. [S1,S2]

coverage.heading: How it developed
coverage.answer: The preceding Southern Airways contract specified 24 weekly round trips with nine-seat aircraft. In 2024 five carriers submitted proposals; DOT chose DAC in March 2025. Those are historical bidders, not a 2026 shortlist. [S2]

coverage.heading: What is happening now
coverage.answer: The supplied Fly Pueblo notice invites residents to meet bidding airlines. The airport still lists DAC; verify the proposed schedules and attendance with airport staff. [S1,S4]

coverage.heading: Important dates
coverage.answer: March 17, 2025 selection order; April 1, 2025 contract start; December 15, 2026 open house 11 am–1 pm; March 31, 2027 scheduled contract end. New order and comment cutoff not established. [S1,S2]

coverage.heading: Who is affected
coverage.answer: Potential passengers, families, employers, students, airport workers, visitors and residents of the surrounding region. Quantify actual users and unmet demand rather than assuming all residents benefit.

coverage.heading: Children and future generations
coverage.answer: Assess travel for specialist appointments, educational trips, family reunification, and access to aviation career pathways. Track affordability and cancellations without collecting children's personal details; no measured child outcome yet.

coverage.heading: Families and workers
coverage.answer: Compare door-to-door costs, work time lost, missed connections, accessible transport and baggage costs. A household without a car may face different choices from one driving to Denver.

coverage.heading: Neighborhoods and wider region
coverage.answer: Pueblo Memorial is east of the city. Include Pueblo West and southeastern Colorado in a voluntary origin survey; do not assign the whole region's demand to the airport. [S11]

coverage.heading: Fairness and access
coverage.answer: Ask each bidder for wheelchair boarding arrangements, accessible lavatories where applicable, assistance procedures, accessible booking and fares; evaluate actual performance, not aircraft size alone.

coverage.heading: Who is responsible
coverage.answer: City Aviation manages local airport operations; carriers deliver service; U.S. DOT administers the EAS award. Airport Advisory Committee provides recommendations. [S3,S9,S11]

coverage.heading: Who can make decisions
coverage.answer: DOT selects the provider; City officials and actual or prospective passengers can submit preferences. The open house itself is not a final vote or award. [S3]

coverage.heading: Rules and requirements
coverage.answer: DOT describes an average of at least 10 enplanements per service day for communities not exempt by distance, and a subsidy-per-passenger threshold below $650 for communities less than 175 miles from the nearest large or medium hub. Confirm Pueblo's official distance and calculation. [S3]

coverage.heading: Promises and commitments
coverage.answer: Current order specifies twelve nonstop weekly round trips to Denver, 30- or 50-seat aircraft; scheduled service is not the same as completed service. [S2]

coverage.heading: Oversight and accountability
coverage.answer: Seek the next selection order, local recommendation, comment summary, contract compliance, and Airport Advisory Committee records. Separate city lease and federal EAS contract. [S2,S3,S9]

coverage.heading: Where money comes from
coverage.answer: The EAS subsidy is federally funded. Municipal operations, leases, capital grants and local matching funds have separate accounting. Do not assign the airline subsidy to the City's general fund. [S2,S3]

coverage.heading: Costs to public and households
coverage.answer: Existing second-year annual subsidy rate is $6,836,498. Household cost should include ticket, parking, ground transport, time, baggage and expected disruption; no current fare quote is implied. [S2]

coverage.heading: What has been approved
coverage.answer: Order 2025-3-7 specifies year-one $6,449,526 and year-two $6,836,498, a nominal two-year total of $13,286,024. Future bid amounts not verified. [S2]

coverage.heading: What has actually been paid
coverage.answer: DOT generally compensates compliant completed segments after service. Obtain actual claims, adjustments, payments and fiscal-year denominator; the announced annual subsidy is not proof of cash disbursement. [S3]

coverage.heading: Benefits and value
coverage.answer: CDOT's 2025 study estimates 838 jobs and $226.095m business revenue associated with the overall airport. These figures include wider aviation activity and are not a measure of EAS-only benefit or loss. [S5,S6]

coverage.heading: How the service works
coverage.answer: Air carriers submit proposals for routes, schedule, equipment and requested support; DOT solicits preferences and evaluates the statutory factors before selecting. [S3]

coverage.heading: Capacity and availability
coverage.answer: Current contracted frequency implies 624 scheduled departures per 52-week illustrative year, each 30 or 50 seats, or 18,720–31,200 outbound seats before actual schedule deviations. Do not confuse available seats with people flown. [S2]

coverage.heading: Quality and actual results
coverage.answer: Publish monthly completion and on-time rates, actual boardings, accessible-service metrics and missed connection reports. A secondary route compilation reports low utilization, but official EAS metrics remain unverified. [S12]

coverage.heading: Reliability and maintenance
coverage.answer: Compare spare aircraft, replacement crew, weather planning, incident procedures and hub recovery as service-quality considerations. Do not suggest operations in unsafe conditions.

coverage.heading: Delays and obstacles
coverage.answer: Key unknowns are the formal solicitation, bidder identities, proposed schedules, airport performance, applicable waivers and official award timing. [S10]

coverage.heading: Connections to other issues
coverage.answer: Rail, buses, highway travel, tourism, workforce training, economic development, airport capital planning and regional fiscal resilience are interconnected but distinct funding instruments.

coverage.heading: Energy and resource needs
coverage.answer: Compare measured fuel per passenger trip and airport operating resources across equivalent itineraries, including driving to substitute airports. No energy score without data.

coverage.heading: Environmental and physical effects
coverage.answer: Assess noise, air emissions, airport pavement, water and stormwater obligations through appropriate official studies. No new construction or quantified environmental impact is established by the open house.

coverage.heading: Risks and unintended effects
coverage.answer: Low ridership, rising subsidy, insufficient connection windows, affordability barriers or service gaps may create feedback loops. These are conditional risks, not findings.

coverage.heading: Long-term consequences
coverage.answer: Continued useful connectivity could support workforce and business access; loss of service could increase road travel. A scheduled airline disruption does not imply closure of general aviation, cargo or training.

coverage.heading: Available alternatives
coverage.answer: Compare any actual bids, a continued Denver link, other viable hub proposals, alternate EAS only if available and authorized, and ground connections as contingency. No alternative described here is a confirmed bid.

coverage.heading: Tradeoffs between options
coverage.answer: Balance frequency, larger aircraft, competitive fares, accessible boarding, reliable connections, subsidy and transition risk. Avoid recommending a carrier before seeing comparable bids.

coverage.heading: Lessons from elsewhere
coverage.answer: Use similar EAS communities as benchmarks only after normalizing geography, service days, aircraft and passenger reporting; no peer performance claim is made.

coverage.heading: What could improve the situation
coverage.answer: Create a common bid table, publish monthly performance and eligibility data, survey unused demand, and test last-mile airport transport. Start with existing data resources and reversible pilots.

coverage.heading: What people can do
coverage.answer: Attend the December 15 event; call 719-553-2760 if unable to attend and ask how to submit written comments plus the official deadline. Use the known DOT docket number to find filed material. [S1,S10,S11]

coverage.heading: How strong the evidence is
coverage.answer: Contract and national rules are primary official sources. Event date is supported by supplied announcement only; latest bid documents and eligibility calculations not retrieved. Study economic values are estimates.

coverage.heading: Conflicting information and other explanations
coverage.answer: In 2024 the City favored Breeze but DOT selected DAC after weighing criteria including cost. Public preference matters but is not dispositive. Current performance requires current evidence. [S2]

coverage.heading: What remains unknown
coverage.answer: FY2026 DOT passenger denominator, actual eligible payments, waiver history, 2026 bidders, local operating net cost, response plans, comment procedure and future award.

coverage.heading: What would change the conclusion
coverage.answer: New solicitation or award, formal eligibility/waiver status, audited performance data, city recommendation, updated event notice or documented route economics trigger an amendment.

coverage.heading: Qified insight
coverage.answer: Treat commercial air service as a bounded regional access system: service design influences ridership, ridership affects funding resilience, and funding affects connectivity. Protect separate airport functions and test service options against documented household and public costs.

q.T2Y: Separate sourced facts and unknowns; yield is a public bid comparison, comment guide and records checklist.
q.EE: Compute only from compatible energy and cost observations; compare existing data before new spending.
q.RX: Keep prior dated evidence and add amendments; recheck notice and bid status weekly and around event/award.
q.eventHorizon: Review Dec 15 and Dec 16–22, mid-January, and March 31/April 1; no automatic monitoring.
q.leap: Unified accessible mobility and workforce planning, initially a reversible shared dashboard.
q.shock: Model service interruption with advance notices and ground alternatives; no claim it will occur.
q.supervision: Human editorial review and no carrier ranking until verified bids.
